purpose: Document Russian attacks, disabling attempts and occupation-linked control of Ukrainian radio/television distribution infrastructure during the full-scale invasion, preserving distinctions between destruction, temporary outage, seizure and source substitution.
claim_ceiling: Russia repeatedly targeted Ukrainian broadcast infrastructure from the opening days of the 2022 invasion.
Some attacks directly interrupted television/radio access; occupied areas also saw seizure and substitution of broadcast infrastructure.
Attacks on nearby energy infrastructure can impair broadcasting, but a specific intent to disable a given tower through a given substation must be separately evidenced.
The pattern demonstrates that information distribution remains a target; it does not by itself prove every strike on nearby civilian infrastructure was intended to suppress media.

documented_cases.finding: Russian forces struck Kyiv's TV tower, killing five people including camera operator Yevhenii Sakun. The attack interrupted 32 TV channels and several dozen radio stations; CPJ reported damage to the tower control room and an electrical substation. Russia's Defense Ministry had shortly beforehand announced strikes intended to stop alleged informational attacks.
RSF documented Russian strikes on TV/radio towers in Kharkiv, Lysychansk and Korosten immediately after the Kyiv strike, suspending or terminating broadcasts.
Russian forces shelled the television tower in Orikhiv, which carried more than twenty national and regional channels according to Ukrainian media monitoring.
During a nine-missile attack on Zaporizhzhia, one missile fell near the television tower in the city center according to the regional administration, as preserved by IMI.
documented_cases.claim_limit: The public evidence supports proximity to the tower; exact targeting intent is not independently established in this artifact.

documented_cases.finding: A Russian air strike destroyed the main mast of Kharkiv's 240-meter television tower and interrupted digital television service. Reuters reported that the tower had also been targeted earlier in 2022.
A Russian drone attack damaged Suspilne Zaporizhzhia premises and the television tower, temporarily taking television broadcasting off air. No staff were killed because personnel had taken shelter.

occupation_control_parallel.finding: Where Russia gained territorial control, physical damage was complemented by seizure of transmitters/frequencies, replacement of Ukrainian programming with Russian-aligned content, and in 2022+ rerouting of Internet connectivity through Russian networks.

publicly_supported: missile landed near Zaporizhzhia city TV tower 2022-09-22
Zaporizhzhia TV tower damaged and broadcasting temporarily lost 2026-05-13
zaporizhzhia_note.not_yet_promoted: A specific claim that earlier Zaporizhzhia electrical-substation attacks were operationally intended to disable this exact TV tower remains unverified in the sources recovered in this pass.

transfer_to_tspu_warning: Repeated physical targeting of broadcast distribution strengthens the historical claim that controlling or denying the information-distribution layer is operationally important. A distributed digital control system could reproduce some source-denial functions without physically destroying a tower, but only where it actually controls the relevant user traffic path.
next_gates: Reconstruct all Ukrainian tower/transmitter strikes by date, node and service outage from 2022-2026.
Map energy dependencies of major broadcast nodes without disclosing exploitable infrastructure detail; use only public historical outage evidence.
Separate accidental collateral damage from announced or repeated targeting of broadcast infrastructure.
Compare denial-only attacks with occupation cases where source substitution followed.
